column2: When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
the dear son of Odysseus rose from his bed,
put on his clothes, and slung a sharp sword about his shoulder,
and under his shining feet bound fair sandals,
and went to go out from his chamber, like a god to look upon.
At once he ordered the clear-voiced heralds
to call the long-haired Achaeans to assembly.
They made the call, and the others gathered very quickly.
But when they had gathered and were assembled together,
he went to the assembly, holding a bronze spear in his hand,
not alone; two swift-footed dogs followed along with him.
And Athena poured upon him a marvellous grace,
and all the people marvelled at him as he came up.
He sat in his father's seat, and the elders gave way.
Then among them the hero Aegyptius began to speak,
who was bent with age and knew countless things.
For his dear son had gone with godlike Odysseus
to Ilios of the fine horses in the hollow ships,
the spearman Antiphos; but the savage Cyclops killed him
in his hollow cave, and made him his last supper.
He had three others: one consorted with the suitors,
Eurynomos, and two always kept their father's works.
But not even so did he forget him, grieving and sorrowing.
Shedding tears for him he spoke out and said among them:

Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I shall say.
26	Never has our assembly or seat been held
27	since godlike Odysseus went in the hollow ships.
28	But now who has summoned us thus? What need comes so great
29	upon one of the younger men or of those who are older?
30	Has he heard some report of an army coming,
31	which he could tell us plainly, having learned it first?
32	Or does he make known and speak of some other public matter?
33	He seems to me a good man, a blessed one. May Zeus
34	fulfil for him some good, whatever he desires in his mind.
So he spoke, and the dear son of Odysseus rejoiced at the omen,
and no longer sat for long, but was eager to speak;
he stood in the middle of the assembly; and the sceptre
the herald Peisenor, who knew wise counsels, placed in his hand.
Then, addressing the old man first, he spoke:

Old man, that man is not far off, and soon you will know yourself,
41	the one who gathered the people; and grief comes to me most of all.
42	I have heard no report of an army coming,
43	which I could tell you plainly, having learned it first,
44	nor do I make known or speak of any other public matter,
45	but my own need, that evils have fallen on my house,
46	two of them: one, that I have lost my noble father, who once among you
47	here was king, and was gentle as a father;
48	and now again a far greater one, which soon the whole house
49	will utterly ruin, and will destroy my livelihood altogether.
50	Suitors have pressed upon my mother, against her will,
51	dear sons of the men who are here the best,
52	who shrink from going to the house of her father
53	Icarius, so that he himself might arrange the bride-gifts for his daughter
54	and give her to whom he wishes and who comes in favour to him;
55	but they, frequenting our house all the days,
56	sacrificing oxen and sheep and fat goats,
57	feast and drink the sparkling wine
58	wantonly; and most of it is consumed. For there is no man,
59	such as Odysseus was, to ward off the curse from the house.
60	And we are in no way such as to ward it off; surely even afterwards
61	we shall be wretched and men untaught in valour.
62	Indeed I would defend myself, if power were at hand for me.
63	For deeds no longer endurable have been done, and no longer fairly
64	is my house destroyed. Feel shame yourselves,
65	and respect the other men who live around,
66	the neighbours; and fear the wrath of the gods,
67	lest they turn upon you in indignation at your evil deeds.
68	I beseech you by Olympian Zeus and by Themis,
69	who both looses and seats the assemblies of men:
70	stop, friends, and leave me alone to be worn
71	by bitter grief, unless somewhere my father, good Odysseus,
72	in ill-will did evil to the well-greaved Achaeans,
73	for which you, taking requital, do me evil in ill-will,
74	urging these men on. But better would it be for me
75	that you yourselves eat up my treasures and my flocks.
76	If you were to eat, there might soon be some recompense;
77	for in the meantime we would go about the town pressing with words,
78	demanding back our goods, until everything was given back.
79	But now you cast upon my heart pains that have no outcome.
So he spoke in anger, and threw the sceptre to the ground,
bursting out in tears; and pity took all the people.
Then all the others were silent, and not one dared
answer Telemachus with harsh words;
but Antinous alone answered him and spoke:

Telemachus, high-talker, of unrestrained fury, what have you said,
86	shaming us; you would like to fasten blame on us.
87	It is not the Achaean suitors who are to blame to you,
88	but your dear mother, who knows crafty schemes beyond others.
89	For it is already the third year, and soon the fourth is coming,
90	since she has been cheating the hearts in the breasts of the Achaeans.
91	She raises hopes in all and makes promises to each man,
92	sending messages, but her mind intends other things.
93	And she devised in her mind this other trick as well:
94	having set up a great loom in the halls, she wove,
95	a fine and ample web; and at once she said among us:
96	'Young men, my suitors, since godlike Odysseus has died,
97	wait, though eager for my marriage, until I finish
98	this robe, lest my threads perish in vain,
99	a shroud for the hero Laertes, for when
100	the ruinous fate of long-lasting death shall bring him down,
101	lest any of the Achaean women in the district be indignant with me,
102	if he lie without a shroud, having gathered so many possessions.'
103	So she spoke, and our proud heart was persuaded.
104	Then by day she would weave the great web,
105	and by night unravel it, when she had set torches beside her.
106	So for three years she escaped notice by her trick and persuaded the Achaeans;
107	but when the fourth year came and the seasons came round,
108	then at last one of the women, who knew it clearly, spoke,
109	and we found her unravelling the glorious web.
110	So she finished it, against her will, by compulsion.
111	To you the suitors answer thus, that you may know
112	in your own heart, and all the Achaeans may know:
113	send your mother away, and bid her marry
114	whomever her father bids and who pleases her.
115	But if she will still vex the sons of the Achaeans for long,
116	pondering in her heart the things that Athena gave her beyond others,
117	to know exceedingly beautiful works and good wits
118	and cunning, such as we have not heard of even among the ancients,
119	of those who were before, the fair-tressed Achaean women,
120	Tyro and Alcmene and fair-crowned Mycene;
121	none of these had thoughts like Penelope's;
122	but this at least she did not devise rightly.
123	For so long they will eat your livelihood and possessions,
124	as long as she keeps that mind which the gods now
125	put in her breast. Great fame for herself
126	she makes, but for you a longing for your much livelihood.
127	We shall neither go to our works before, nor anywhere else,
128	until she marries whichever of the Achaeans she wishes.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

Antinous, there is no way to thrust out of the house against her will
131	her who bore me, who reared me; and my father is elsewhere on the earth,
132	whether he lives or is dead; and it is hard for me to pay back much
133	to Icarius, if I of my own will send my mother away.
134	For from her father I shall suffer evils, and another the deity
135	will give, since my mother will call on the hateful Erinyes
136	as she leaves the house; and blame will come to me from men;
137	so I shall never speak this word.
138	But if your own heart is indignant at it,
139	go out of my halls, and prepare other feasts,
140	eating your own possessions, taking turns from house to house.
141	But if this seems to you better and preferable,
142	that one man's livelihood should perish unpaid for,
143	devour it; and I shall call upon the gods who are for ever,
144	in case Zeus somewhere grants that deeds of requital come to pass.
145	Unpaid for you would then perish inside the house.
So spoke Telemachus, and for him wide-seeing Zeus
sent two eagles to fly from on high, from the peak of a mountain.
For a time they flew on the breath of the wind,
close to one another, with wings outstretched;
but when they came to the middle of the noisy assembly,
there wheeling round they shook their thick wings,
and looked down on the heads of all, and their look was destruction;
and tearing with their talons each other's cheeks and necks around,
they darted off to the right through the houses and the city.
And they marvelled at the birds, when they saw them with their eyes,
and pondered in their hearts what was going to be fulfilled.
And among them spoke the old hero Halitherses,
son of Mastor; for he alone surpassed his age-mates
in knowing birds and speaking what was fated;
he with good thought spoke out and said among them:

Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I shall say;
162	and to the suitors above all I speak, declaring this;
163	for a great calamity rolls upon them; for Odysseus
164	will not be long away from his dear ones, but already somewhere,
165	being near, he is sowing slaughter and doom for these
166	all; and for many others also there will be evil,
167	who inhabit sunny Ithaca. But long before that
168	let us consider how we may stop them; and let them themselves
169	stop; for this is at once better for them.
170	For I prophesy not untried, but knowing well;
171	for I say that for him too everything has been fulfilled,
172	as I told him, when the Argives embarked for Ilios,
173	and with them went Odysseus of many wiles.
174	I said that after suffering many evils, having lost all his comrades,
175	unrecognized by all, in the twentieth year
176	he would come home; and now all this is being fulfilled.
Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered him in turn:

Old man, come now, go home and prophesy to your children,
179	lest they somewhere suffer some evil hereafter;
180	but in these matters I am far better than you at prophesying.
181	Many birds go about under the rays of the sun,
182	and not all are meaningful; but Odysseus
183	has perished far away, as you too ought to have perished
184	with him. You would not prophesy so much,
185	nor would you urge Telemachus, angered, on thus,
186	expecting a gift for your house, if he should provide it.
187	But I will tell you, and this shall also be accomplished:
188	if you, knowing many ancient things, a younger man
189	beguiling with words, rouse him to be angry,
190	first, it will be more grievous for him himself,
191	and he will not be able to accomplish anything because of these men;
192	and on you, old man, we shall lay a fine, which in your heart
193	you will be vexed to pay; and the pain will be hard for you.
194	And I myself will advise Telemachus before all:
195	let him bid his mother go back to her father;
196	and they will prepare the marriage and make ready gifts
197	very many, as many as befit a dear daughter to follow.
198	For I do not think the sons of the Achaeans will stop
199	from their painful wooing, since we fear no one in any case,
200	neither Telemachus, though he be very talkative,
201	nor do we heed the prophecy which you, old man,
202	utter unaccomplished, and you become still more hated.
203	And the goods will be badly eaten up, and never will they be
204	made good, so long as she keeps putting off the Achaeans
205	about her marriage; and we, waiting all our days,
206	contend because of her excellence, and do not go after other women,
207	whom it is fitting for each of us to marry.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

Eurymachus, and you others, as many as are proud suitors,
210	about these things I no longer beseech you nor speak;
211	for the gods already know them, and all the Achaeans.
212	But come, give me a swift ship and twenty companions,
213	who may accomplish a path for me hither and thither.
214	For I shall go to Sparta and to sandy Pylos
215	to enquire about the return of my father, long gone,
216	in case some mortal tells me, or I hear a rumour
217	from Zeus, which most of all brings fame to men.
218	If I hear that my father is alive and returning,
219	then, worn down though I am, I could endure still a year;
220	but if I hear that he is dead and no longer exists,
221	then, returning to my dear native land,
222	I shall heap up a mound for him and perform funeral rites
223	very many, as is fitting, and give my mother to a husband.
So saying he sat down, and among them rose
Mentor, who was a companion of blameless Odysseus,
and to whom, going in the ships, he entrusted the whole house,
to obey the old man and to keep everything secure;
he with good thought spoke out and said among them:

Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I shall say.
230	Let no sceptre-holding king any longer be willingly
231	kind and gentle, nor know in his mind what is right,
232	but let him always be harsh and do wicked things;
233	since no one remembers godlike Odysseus
234	of the people over whom he ruled, and he was gentle as a father.
235	But indeed I do not begrudge the proud suitors
236	doing violent deeds by the evil devising of their mind;
237	for staking their own heads they violently devour
238	the house of Odysseus, saying that he will no longer return.
239	But now I am indignant at the rest of the people, how all of you
240	sit speechless, and not by attacking with words
241	do you stop the few suitors, though you are many.
Then Leocritus, son of Euenor, answered him in turn:

Mentor, mischievous, witless in mind, what have you said,
244	urging us to stop. But it is hard
245	to fight even against more men over a feast.
246	For even if Odysseus of Ithaca himself came
247	and in his own house were minded in his heart to drive out
248	from the hall the proud suitors as they feasted,
249	his wife would not rejoice at his coming, though she longs for him greatly,
250	but there he would meet an unseemly fate,
251	if he fought against more; you have not spoken according to what is right.
252	But come, people, scatter each to his work,
253	and for this man Mentor and Halitherses will speed the journey,
254	who from the beginning are his father's companions.
255	But I think that, sitting long, he will learn the news
256	in Ithaca, and will never complete this journey.
So he spoke, and quickly broke up the assembly.
They scattered, each to his own house,
and the suitors went to the house of godlike Odysseus.
But Telemachus, going apart to the shore of the sea,
washed his hands in the grey salt water and prayed to Athena:

Hear me, god who came yesterday to our house,
263	and bade me go in a ship over the misty sea
264	to enquire about the return of my father, long gone;
265	but all this the Achaeans delay,
266	and the suitors most of all, wickedly overbearing.
So he spoke praying, and Athena came near him,
likened to Mentor in form and in voice,
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

Telemachus, not hereafter will you be bad nor senseless,
271	if indeed the good strength of your father has been instilled in you,
272	such as he was in accomplishing both deed and word,
273	then the voyage will not be vain for you nor unaccomplished.
274	But if you are not the offspring of him and Penelope,
275	then I do not expect that you will accomplish what you intend.
276	For few sons are like their father,
277	the more are worse, and few are better than their father.
278	But since hereafter you will be neither bad nor senseless,
279	and the cunning of Odysseus has not altogether left you,
280	there is hope then that you will accomplish these deeds.
281	Therefore now leave the counsel and the mind of the suitors,
282	foolish ones, since they are in no way sensible or just;
283	nor do they know at all of death and black doom,
284	which is indeed near them, for all to perish in one day.
285	And the journey you intend will not long be far from you;
286	for such a companion of your father am I,
287	who will fit out a swift ship for you and follow myself.
288	But you go to the house and mingle with the suitors,
289	and prepare provisions and put everything into vessels,
290	wine in jars, and barley-meal, the marrow of men,
291	in thick skins; and I through the district will
292	quickly gather companions, volunteers. And there are ships
293	many in sea-girt Ithaca, new and old;
294	of these I will look over for you whichever is the best,
295	and quickly, having fitted it out, we shall launch it on the broad sea.
So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus; and no longer long
did Telemachus linger, when he heard the voice of the goddess.
He went to go to the house, grieved in his dear heart,
and found the proud suitors in the halls,
flaying goats and singeing fat swine in the courtyard.
And Antinous, laughing, went straight to Telemachus,
and clung to his hand, and spoke a word and called him by name:

Telemachus, high-talker, of unrestrained fury, let no other
304	evil be a care in your breast, either deed or word,
305	but eat and drink with me, as before.
306	And all these things the Achaeans will accomplish for you,
307	a ship and chosen oarsmen, that you may come the sooner
308	to holy Pylos in search of news of your noble father.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

Antinous, it is not possible among you overweening ones
311	to feast in silence and to be glad at ease.
312	Is it not enough that before you wasted many fine
313	possessions of mine, suitors, when I was still a child?
314	But now that I am big and hear the word of others
315	and learn, and my spirit grows within me,
316	I shall try to hurl evil dooms on you,
317	either going to Pylos, or here in this very district.
318	I shall go, and the journey I speak of will not be in vain,
319	as a passenger; for I do not command a ship or oarsmen:
320	so it seemed to you somehow to be more profitable.
He spoke, and easily drew his hand from the hand of Antinous;
and the suitors in the house were preparing the feast.
And they mocked and taunted him with words.
And thus would one of the overweening young men say:

Truly Telemachus is planning slaughter for us.
326	Either he will bring helpers from sandy Pylos
327	or even from Sparta, since he is terribly eager;
328	or he even wishes to go to Ephyra, the rich land,
329	to bring from there life-destroying drugs,
330	and throw them in the mixing-bowl and destroy us all.
And another of the overweening young men would say:

Who knows whether he himself, going in a hollow ship,
333	might perish far from his dear ones, wandering like Odysseus?
334	So he would even add more labour for us;
335	for we would divide all his possessions, and the house
336	we would give to his mother to keep, and to whoever marries her.
So they spoke; and he went down to his father's high-roofed
wide storeroom, where gold and bronze lay in a heap,
and clothing in chests, and fragrant olive oil in plenty;
and in it were jars of old sweet-drinking wine,
stood, holding unmixed divine drink within,
in a row against the wall, in case Odysseus ever
should come home, even after suffering many pains.
And closed doors were fitted tightly,
double doors; and within a woman, a housekeeper, night and day
kept watch, who guarded everything with her abundant understanding of mind,
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor.
Her then Telemachus addressed, having called her to the chamber:

Nurse, come, draw me wine in jars,
350	sweet, the one that is most pleasant after the one you keep
351	expecting that ill-fated man, in case from somewhere should come
352	Zeus-born Odysseus, having escaped death and the dooms.
353	Fill twelve, and fit lids on them all.
354	And pour barley-meal for me into well-sewn skins;
355	let there be twenty measures of mill-ground barley-meal.
356	And you alone know; let all be gathered together;
357	for in the evening I shall fetch it, when
358	my mother goes up to her upper room and thinks of bed.
359	For I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos
360	to enquire about the return of my dear father, if I may hear anywhere.
So he spoke, and the dear nurse Eurycleia cried out,
and lamenting spoke to him winged words:

Why, dear child, has this thought come
364	into your mind? Where do you wish to go over the wide earth,
365	being an only, beloved son? And he perished far from his homeland,
366	Zeus-born Odysseus, in a land of strangers.
367	And these, as soon as you go, will plan evils afterwards,
368	so that you perish by guile, and they will themselves divide all this.
369	But stay here sitting among your own; there is no need for you
370	to suffer evils on the unharvested sea, nor to wander.
Then wise Telemachus answered her in turn:

Take heart, nurse, since this plan is not without a god.
373	But swear not to tell this to my dear mother,
374	until the eleventh or twelfth day comes,
375	or she herself misses me and hears that I have set out,
376	so that she may not mar her fair skin with weeping.
So he spoke, and the old woman swore the great oath of the gods.
But when she had sworn and completed the oath,
at once then she drew wine for him in jars,
and poured barley-meal for him into well-sewn skins.
And Telemachus, going into the house, mingled with the suitors.
Then the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, thought of another thing.
Likened to Telemachus she went everywhere through the city,
and standing beside each man spoke a word,
and bade them gather at evening by the swift ship.
And she asked of Noemon, glorious son of Phronios,
a swift ship; and he readily promised it to her.
And the sun set and all the ways were shadowed,
and then she drew the swift ship down to the sea, and in it all
she placed the gear which well-benched ships carry.
And she stood it at the far end of the harbour, and around it the good companions
gathered in a crowd; and the goddess urged on each.
Then the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, thought of another thing.
She went to go to the house of godlike Odysseus;
there she poured sweet sleep on the suitors,
and made them wander as they drank, and cast the cups from their hands.
And they hastened to sleep throughout the city, and no longer long
did they sit, since sleep fell upon their eyelids.
And to Telemachus spoke grey-eyed Athena,
having called him out from the well-inhabited halls,
likened to Mentor in form and in voice:
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way
swiftly; and he then followed in the footsteps of the goddess.
But when they came down to the ship and the sea,
they found then on the shore the long-haired companions.
And among them spoke the sacred might of Telemachus:

Come, friends, let us bring the provisions; for already all
411	are gathered together in the hall. My mother has learned nothing,
412	nor the other maids; only one heard the word.
So speaking he led the way, and they followed together.
And they, bringing everything, on the well-benched ship
laid it down, as the dear son of Odysseus bade.
Then Telemachus went aboard the ship, and Athena led,
and she sat down in the stern of the ship; and near her
sat Telemachus. And they loosed the stern cables,
and themselves went aboard and sat down on the benches.
And grey-eyed Athena sent them a favourable wind,
the clear Zephyr, singing over the wine-dark sea.
And Telemachus urged on his companions and bade them
take hold of the tackle; and they obeyed his urging.
They raised the mast of fir and set it up inside the hollow mast-holder,
and bound it with forestays,
and hoisted the white sails with well-twisted ox-hide ropes.
And the wind filled the middle of the sail, and around the cutwater
the dark wave roared loudly as the ship went on;
and she ran over the wave, accomplishing her way.
And having made fast the tackle throughout the swift black ship,
they set up mixing-bowls brimmed with wine,
and poured libations to the immortal gods who are for ever,
and above all of them to the grey-eyed daughter of Zeus.
All night long, and into the dawn, she cut her way.
